changes.before: Change view[0]=9 to view[1]=9. What does the unchanged print show?
changes.after: Use a slice to view items stored in an array.

before: A slice carries a reference to underlying array storage plus length and capacity. Assigning a slice copies this descriptor, not all its elements.
values[1:3] includes indices 1 and 2, excluding 3. Updating view[0] updates the underlying element at values[1].

len(view) gives the accessible length. Capacity is a separate concept used for reslicing and growth.

The initialized view below covers two elements, so len(view) returns 2, not the three-element owner length and not the last valid view index.
```go
package main
import "fmt"
func main() {
    values := []int{2, 4, 6}
    view := values[1:3]
    fmt.Println(len(view))
}
```
Expected output: 2.
Changing a shared element is visible through any overlapping slice or array view.
Expected output or behavior: 9. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Draw the slice start and length, then map each valid slice index to the underlying array. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A slice describes part of an array: where it starts, its length, and its capacity. Copying a slice copies that description, so the slices can still share their stored items.
`values[1:3]` starts at index 1 and stops before index 3. The new view's index 0 points to values[1]. Its index 1 points to values[2].
`len(view)` counts the items you can use in the slice. Here it is 2. Capacity describes how far the slice can extend within the same array; the next lesson explains it.
Changing an item through one slice changes the shared item. Another view of that same item can see the change.
The screen shows `9`. Changing view[0] changes the same stored item that values[1] reads.
Change the assignment to view[1]. That index points to values[2], while the display line still reads values[1].

before.question: Change view[0]=9 to view[1]=9. What does the unchanged print show?
choices: 9 because every view index selects the same element.
4 because the update now selects values[2].
before.explanation: The slice starts at original index 1, so its second element is original index 2.

after.question: Change view[0] = 9 to view[1] = 9. What does the same display line show?
choices: 9, because every view index means the same item.
6, because the end boundary is included.
after.explanation: view[1] points to values[2]. values[1] keeps its original value, 4.
